author: potuz
content: FWIW I did not mean to sound like talking "down" at you <@840207942581747712> but rather I think that formal verification methods are better used "one step above". I think it'd be great to have a formally verified forkchoice specification.. be absolutely certain that 1/3 of the stake is slashable if two contending branches finalize, be certain that justification is strictly increasing, etc.. I think it becomes much harder to have these methods being useful at the client level. There's a push to have the pure STF to be formally verified, mostly in the lean world where the STF itself will be a black box that even node implementers would not be able to understand nor diagnose. But as <@543900561460822016> correctly points out, a node is much more than the core STF, and our bugs are typically outside of there

author: sky.cactus
content: There should be no single "ground truth".  If spec, tests, or clients disagree with any of the others, then intelligent reasoning beings who know the *intent* should stop and analyze the situation and decide which is the correct one.  We should be careful to *never* blindly follow any one source (even a specification).

author: taulepton_
content:
Just wanted to chime in and share my experience with evm-sail: https://github.com/frisitano/evm-sail/tree/main. evm-sail is an AI-assisted experiment to formally specify the stateless guest program used for execution proofs on Ethereum.  The ambition was to generate a spec that is readable, formal, comprehensive, executable, performant and extracts to a number of proof assistant backends. For this experiment, I used Sail, which is an architecture definition language. I developed an SMT-based compiler for evm-sail that achieved performance comparable to other production client guest programs: https://frisitano.github.io/evm-sail/performance.html.  We have spec extractions in Lean and Rocq.

Just to throw out a few remarks/talking points:
- To formally verify, first you must formally specify
- What makes a formal specification authoritative? Is it reviews from a broad set of collaborators? Is it proven agreement of the spec with a diverse set of implementations? Is it proven agreement amongst a broad set of formal specifications?
- What is your formal verification target? Is it a client's source code (in which case you are trusting the compiler)? Is it the binary itself?  If you are FV'ing the binary, then how do you handle inlining and mangling from the compiler?
- Are you willing to just blindly trust AI-written proofs that no human could ever comprehend?

author: taulepton_
content:
These are just a few questions that arise once you open the FV can of worms, but there is certainly value here imo. I have my own opinion on these questions and personally believe systems-level languages and proof assistants must merge into one. A bit like how Rust gave us memory-safety, these new languages should give us "semantic safety" - the same source code and environment can compile to both assembly and proofs. I have some agents working on a language of this nature, which I would describe as a systems-level protocol specification language, but it's highly experimental and speculative. 

Anyway, I digress; I think we should encourage client teams to adopt FV. A small, conservatively scoped initiative to collaborate and share insights and findings as a feasibility analysis. If successful, we can continue the effort to deepen integration with FV and harden clients over time as we learn. 

Idea: Choose a small component of a client's STF; each team writes a formal specification for said component. Each team FV's that their spec is consistent with their source code. Teams are paired and must prove that their specs are consistent.

author: sproul
content:
I’ve been trying to formally verify parts of Lighthouse and it is slow going, even with AI assistance.

So far I’ve managed:

- Lean version of xdelta3 (too slow to use)
- C version of xdelta3 verified in Isabelle/HOL (took fucking forever, do not recommend, still slower than the original)
- First steps verifying Milhouse the data structure library used by Lighthouse (https://github.com/sigp/milhouse/pull/104)

Of these the Milhouse verification is most encouraging. Aeneas lets us translate Rust to high level Lean which is easy to reason about. However Aeneas feels very immature, it has a lot of Rust code that it chokes on for seemingly no good reason, and there are inherent limitations in its design (no unsafe). All the tools I’ve tried have similar issues. However it has uncovered bugs in Milhouse and I’m hoping I’ll be able to use it more broadly.

I’ve previously worked on seL4, and I’m still in contact with a few of the devs. They are painstakingly still proving properties that they had started working on 10y ago, and seL4 is deliberately as small as possible. I think based on this and my experience with LH verification we have to be realistic about what’s achievable with our current budgets and current devs. A full client seems like an impossible lift. A formal spec of the state transition or fork choice might be within reach, followed by a verified implementation. I think verifying *existing* code unchanged is probably close to impossible – for Rust at least you need to simplify and tailor your code to the translation.

I hope to write a blog post about the Milhouse work once it’s done. Will share that here when I do

author: potuz
content:
Formally verifying the Python spec doesn't really mean anything though. What we typically mean by formally verifying the spec is to check that the Python specification satisfies some claimed invariants: no double spending, it costs more to do this attack than what you can get out of it, every block that can broadcast in this time will be able to execute this much gas under this pricing and these execution opcodes timing assumptions (to give an engineering one) etc.  

The issue is to find the right invariants you want to hold
